content: The detection of the Japanese Encephalitis (JE) virus genome can be achieved through reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) or other equally sensitive and specific nucleic acid detection assays, such as loop-mediated isothermal amplification or whole genome sequencing. These methods can be applied to cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), serum, plasma, blood, or brain tissue. Isolation of the JE virus from these same specimens is another diagnostic approach. Additionally, a fourfold or greater rise in JE virus-specific IgG antibody titers, as measured by the plaque reduction neutralization test (PRNT), between acute and convalescent serum samples collected at least 14 days apart, is indicative of recent infection. The interpretation of IgM antibody test results requires caution. A positive IgM result may persist for 30–90 days, and in some cases, even longer. Therefore, a positive IgM result may reflect a past infection or vaccination rather than an active infection. In highly endemic areas, patients with acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) caused by other pathogens may still test positive for JE virus-specific IgM due to a recent subclinical infection. Consequently, testing of CSF samples is recommended for all encephalitis cases, if feasible. Even with a positive CSF result, confirmatory tests should be performed to rule out cross-reactivity with other flaviviruses circulating in the region, especially during ongoing outbreaks of dengue or other flaviviruses, in areas with high JE vaccination coverage, or in regions lacking epidemiological and entomological evidence of JE transmission. For individuals vaccinated against JE within six months prior to illness onset, testing a single serum sample for JE IgM may not be diagnostic, as detected IgM could be vaccine-related. In such cases, diagnosis can only be confirmed by detecting JE IgM in CSF, isolating the JE virus, obtaining a positive nucleic acid amplification test result, performing immunohistochemistry, or demonstrating a fourfold or greater rise in antibody titers between acute and convalescent serum samples. A negative IgM result in serum collected within the first seven days of illness does not rule out JE, as IgM levels may not yet be detectable. In such cases, testing should be repeated on a convalescent-phase serum sample. A fourfold or greater rise in JE virus-specific antibodies between acute and convalescent-phase serum specimens can confirm recent infection. When interpreting results, it is essential to consider the patient’s vaccination history, the timing of symptom onset, and the presence of other flaviviruses in the region that may cause cross-reactivity in serological assays. Virus isolation and nucleic acid amplification tests are not reliable for ruling out JE, as they are insensitive in detecting JE virus or viral RNA in blood or CSF due to the low level of viremia in humans. These methods are more likely to yield positive results in fatal cases, but their sensitivity remains limited. CSF examination results can provide valuable diagnostic clues. A CSF cell count of fewer than 10 cells/mm³, particularly fewer than 6 cells/mm³, may indicate encephalopathy or early bacterial infection. A cell count of 10–100 cells/mm³, predominantly lymphocytic, suggests encephalitis or viral meningitis. A cell count exceeding 100 cells/mm³ with predominantly polymorphonuclear cells is indicative of bacterial meningitis, while a similar count with predominantly lymphocytes points to viral meningitis. High protein concentration (>100 mg/dL) and low glucose levels (<40 mg/dL) in CSF may indicate tuberculous meningitis or another bacterial cause. Laboratory-confirmed JE cases are those in which diagnostic testing has confirmed the presence of JE virus. Probable JE cases occur in close geographical and temporal association with laboratory-confirmed cases during an outbreak. AES cases caused by other agents are those in which diagnostic testing identifies an etiological agent other than JE virus. AES cases of unknown origin are those in which no diagnostic testing was performed, no etiological agent was identified, or test results were inconclusive. JE cannot be ruled out in cases with negative IgM results if the sample was collected less than seven days after illness onset, as IgM levels may not yet be detectable. A second sample should be collected for confirmation. Detection of the virus genome or isolation of the virus in serum, plasma, or blood is highly specific for JE diagnosis but lacks sensitivity, as virus levels are typically undetectable in clinically ill JE cases. Therefore, negative results from these methods should not be used to rule out JE in suspected cases. JE is a vector-borne disease transmitted to humans through the bite of infected Culex mosquitoes, particularly Culex tritaeniorhynchus. The virus is maintained in nature through a cycle involving mosquitoes and vertebrate hosts, primarily pigs and water birds. Humans are incidental hosts and are considered dead-end hosts, as they do not develop high enough viremia to infect feeding mosquitoes. Most infected individuals are asymptomatic, making it challenging to determine the true incidence of JE. It is estimated that less than 1% of those infected with JE virus develop clinical disease. There is no specific antiviral treatment for JE. Management involves supportive care, including hospitalization for close monitoring and addressing potentially life-threatening complications such as raised intracranial pressure, status epilepticus, hypoglycemia, aspiration pneumonia, and secondary infections. Routine supportive care includes rest, fluid intake, fever reduction, and pain relief. Severe cases may require intravenous fluids and vasopressors. JE vaccination should be integrated into national immunization schedules in areas where the disease is a public health priority. Community awareness and education are crucial to reducing delays in seeking medical care and improving outcomes. Vaccination of humans is the only proven method for reducing JE disease. Other measures, such as vaccination of pigs, environmental management for vector control, and chemical control of vectors, have limited evidence of effectiveness. Surveillance data on JE should be used to guide policy and strategies for disease control, assess the impact of vaccination, identify high-risk areas or populations, monitor surveillance and laboratory performance, and evaluate vaccine effectiveness. Surveillance systems should aim for high completeness and timeliness of reporting, adequate specimen collection and transport, and accurate laboratory testing.
